title: India Is About to Put $313 Million Behind Lithium and Nickel Processing. It Wants to Break China's Grip.
excerpt: The Ministry of Mines is expected to unveil a 15 percent capital subsidy for lithium and nickel processing plants — the first dedicated incentive to build refining capacity India has never had.
body:
India is preparing to announce a dedicated incentive programme for lithium and nickel processing, committing roughly ₹30 billion ($313 million) to build domestic refining capacity that the country has never possessed, according to sources familiar with the proposal.

The policy, expected to be unveiled shortly by the Ministry of Mines, would offer a **15 percent capital subsidy** on eligible investments in lithium and nickel processing plants starting on or after 1 April 2026. It represents New Delhi's most direct attempt yet to loosen China's near-total control over the critical minerals that power electric vehicle batteries, renewable energy systems, and advanced electronics.

## The Scale of the Problem

China currently controls roughly 90 percent of global lithium and nickel processing capacity. India, the world's third-largest energy consumer and a country that has set aggressive EV adoption targets — 30 percent for cars and 80 percent for two-wheelers by 2030 — has virtually no refining capability of its own. It imports nearly all of its processed critical minerals, leaving its clean energy transition hostage to a single supplier.

The gap between ambition and infrastructure is stark. India's projected lithium demand is expected to surge from 58 tonnes in 2030 to more than 20,000 tonnes by 2047. Nickel demand is forecast to rise nearly 30-fold in the same period. Without processing plants on Indian soil, every kilowatt-hour of battery capacity will carry a Chinese supply chain behind it.

## What the Policy Offers

Under the proposed scheme, lithium processing plants must have a minimum capacity of 30,000 metric tons to qualify for incentives. Nickel plants need at least 50,000 tons. The subsidies would be available for five years, capped at 40 percent of annual net sales turnover for lithium facilities and 25 percent for nickel.

The government initially plans to support two lithium and two nickel projects — a deliberately constrained rollout designed to anchor domestic capacity before scaling up. The subsidy would be disbursed in stages, contingent on minimum plant utilisation targets set by the government.

Mines Secretary V. L. Kantha Rao had signalled the policy's direction in April, telling reporters that the ministry had shortlisted two critical minerals linked to securing an electric vehicle value chain, without naming them explicitly. Reuters had earlier reported that lithium and nickel were the two minerals under consideration.

## The Broader Strategic Play

The processing incentive is one piece of a larger critical minerals architecture that India has been assembling since 2024. Khanij Bidesh India Ltd., a government-owned entity, has been given a ₹4,500-crore war chest to acquire mineral assets overseas. Separately, ₹500 crore has been earmarked for strategic stockpiling, and ₹1,500 crore for incentivising recyclers who extract minerals from used equipment.

India has also been working the diplomatic track. A deal with Brazil for rare earths and critical minerals was signed under the Pax Silica framework. A free trade agreement with Australia — which holds the world's largest lithium deposits and second-largest cobalt reserves — includes provisions for joint mineral processing. The Australia-India Critical Minerals Research Hub, a collaboration between IIT Hyderabad and Monash University, was approved by India's education ministry earlier this year.

The Union Budget for 2026–27 went further, exempting customs duties on capital goods imports required for critical mineral processing.

## The Diaspora Dimension

For NRIs in the technology and investment sectors, India's critical minerals push opens a new frontier. The country's battery manufacturing ecosystem — already supported by a separate Production Linked Incentive scheme for advanced chemistry cells — now has a potential upstream supply chain to match. Indian-origin executives lead several global battery and EV ventures, and domestic processing capacity could redirect some of that expertise homeward.

The challenge remains execution. India's mining sector has historically struggled with environmental clearances, land acquisition, and bureaucratic delays. Building refining capacity from scratch, in minerals where China has a three-decade head start, will require more than subsidies. It will require speed.

But the policy marks a structural shift. For the first time, India is not merely buying minerals or signing supply agreements. It is investing in the capacity to process them. In a world where control over battery supply chains increasingly determines who builds the next generation of vehicles, grids, and defence systems, that distinction matters.
